reception.text: The lottery drew 16,923 registrants at Miles City, Billings and Sheridan, and 6,500 drew the right to enter.

political_impact.text: Almost no one filed at the $4.00-an-acre price: 263 entries by the end of August, and after a year only 398 entries covering 56,320.75 acres, under six percent of the 969,656.58 acres opened.

later_actions.text: President Taft cut the floor price to $1.50 an acre and ordered an auction of the unsold land.

reception.text: The Wind River lottery drew 10,559 registrants, and 7,240 drew the right to enter.

political_impact.text: After a year, 635 entries covering 94,383.31 acres had been filed, about six percent of the 1,472,844.15 acres opened.
Riverton was born of the opening, platted by the Wyoming Central Irrigation Company, its lots drawn by lottery, and opened August 15, 1906.

legacy.text: The Tenth Circuit held in 2017 that the 1905 act behind this opening diminished the Wind River Reservation, so Riverton is not in Indian country; the Supreme Court declined review in 2018 and the EPA revised its approval in 2019.
Restorations of 1940, 1944 and 1953 helped carry the reservation back past 2.2 million acres.

today.name: Wind River Reservation
today.note: Diminished by the 1905 cession, later partly restored.

related.note: Directed entries on the opened lands to be made at Shoshoni from August 15 through October 3, 1906.

later_actions.text: Congress directed the undisposed-of ceded land restored to the tribes; the restorations were carried out in 1940 and 1944.
The EPA approved the Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho tribes' Clean Air Act treatment-as-a-state application on the view that the 1905 act had not diminished the reservation.
The Tenth Circuit held that Congress diminished the reservation in 1905 and vacated the EPA order.

political_impact.text: Entries on the Shoshone lands were taken at the Shoshoni land office from August 15 through October 3, 1906, then returned to Lander.

related.note: Moved the filing office for the Wind River opening for seven weeks.

political_impact.text: The order restored 8.80 acres to the public domain to cover David Eskelson's homestead entry, which had been erroneously allowed to include two lots of the grazing reserve.

legacy.text: The tribes still held their jointly owned 250,000-acre grazing reserve in 1909, when the government withdrew 56,000 acres of it for the Strawberry Valley reclamation project.

related.note: The 1905 Uintah opening; the grazing reserve was not opened with those lands.

reception.text: Over six days in December 1906, 7,621 sealed bids came in at the Lawton land office, totaling $2,286,300.

political_impact.text: Interior set a floor of $800 a quarter section, $5.00 an acre, and opened and awarded the bids beginning March 15, 1907.

legacy.text: It is often called the last of the great Oklahoma land openings, though it was a sealed-bid sale, not a run.
Oklahoma's Court of Criminal Appeals held in 2021 that Congress disestablished the Kiowa, Comanche and Apache reservation in the Act of June 6, 1900.

uncertain: How much of the Big Pasture and wood reserve was actually sold is not known; only the bid totals are on record.

legacy.text: An act of 1936 let the Secretary of the Interior restore public-domain land to the Walker River Reservation, and part of the 1906 lands came back.

today.name: Walker River Reservation
today.note: Northern Paiute reservation along the lower Walker River north of Walker Lake.

later_actions.text: Congress authorized restoring public-domain land to the reservation.

uncertain: How many acres the October 29, 1906 opening threw open is not known.

reception.text: The Western press covered the openings as opportunity, with registration booths, lottery drawings and overnight boom towns, not as dispossession.

political_impact.text: By 1906 the openings were settled bipartisan policy; debate, where it happened, was over price, irrigation money and land offices, not whether to open the land.
Both big 1906 lotteries drew thousands of registrants and then almost no takers, and both openings were later repriced.

legacy.text: The reservations were left diminished and checkerboarded, and whether surplus-land acts merely opened reservations or shrank them has produced a long line of court cases.
McGirt v. Oklahoma held that only Congress, in plain terms, can disestablish a reservation; it addressed none of these proclamations and was later narrowed by Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta.
legacy.source: McGirt v. Oklahoma, 591 U.S. 894 (2020); Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, 597 U.S. 629 (2022)
